friends_of_longwood_mall_1982.meta_title: 1982: Friends of Longwood Mall | Longwood Mall
friends_of_longwood_mall_1982.title: 1982: Friends of Longwood Mall
paragraphs: On July 15, 1982, the Brookline Chronicle Citizen reported on a neighborhood campaign to save the trees of Longwood Mall, which were then in poor health. Ellen Golde, who 40 years later still leads citizen efforts to look after the trees, led the campaign. It raised over $20,000 (more than $62,000 in 2023 dollars) and persuaded Brookline to match the funds.
In 1984, Friends of Longwood Mall received a Massachusetts Historical Commission Preservation award for their efforts to save the trees.
The full text of the article:
A neighborhood group has come up with a plan to save the nationally-treasured stand of beech trees on Longwood Mall, using both town funds and money raised through private donations.

The trees, planted nearly 150 years ago, are threatened by some twenty years of neglect. A recent review by the Lowden Company of Needham, commissioned by Mall neighbors, shows that four trees are likely to die in the next few years, while the remainder need immediate pruning, fertilizing and cultivation.
After a meeting with Longwood residents Tuesday, the Selectmen said they will ask Town Meeting next spring for $20,000 to rejuvenate the mall's beech trees.
The beech trees were planted on Longwood Mall in 1850 by David Sears, a wealthy Brookline landowner. In 1902, thirteen o his descendants deeded the mall to the town.

Since that time, Longwood Mall has been cited by National Geographic magazine and the Arnold Arboretum as one of the finest single stands of beech trees in the country. The Mall is also listed in the National Register of Historic Places.

When the Sears family turned the Mall over to Brookline, it also turned over responsibility for the care of the valuable beech trees. William Collins, Brookline's assistant director of forestry, estimates the trees were pruned regularly until the mid-1960's. In ears following, Brookline's tree maintenance programs have been all but eliminated in the lace of budget cuts in the forestry budget.
As a result. today all of the trees are growing abnormally slowly, many are brittle and splitting from the sheer weight of their enormous limbs, and several suffer from disease or pest infestation.
*We represent some 70 to 100 abutters and interested people who want to save the mall."
Chatham Street resident Ellen Golde told the Board Tuesday.

Golde's group has volunteered to raise $20,000 (it already has $18.000 in pledges) in private contributions for long-term tree maintenance, it the town will kick in the $20.000 for a "one-time fix" of problems that need immediate attention.

That "one-time fix" would include planting one new beech tree, pruning and fertilizing all the trees, and stringing thick cable in some of the more brittle trees that are cracking and splitting under their own weight.
In return, the privately raised maintenance fund would pay for annual routine upkeep of the mall, including fertilizing, routine pruning, and special spraying for disease and pest control.
The maintenance fund would not be used for certain basic town responsibilities, such as moving and raking. or the removal of dead trees from the mall.
Board of Selectmen Chairman Robert Stein termed the proposal "a superb concept" and Tree-Planting Commission Chairman Hamilton Coolidge thanked the Longwood neighbors for their interest.
*This is the kind of joint commitment by citizens that we like to support," Coolidge said.
Golde called the private contributions "heart-felt money" donated by people who already pay some of the highest residential property taxes in town.
Longwood property owners felt the highest increase in property values and tax bills this year, in part because properties located near the Mall are very desirable.

"Here we are paying more dollars in taxes and vet we're being asked to give over more money for town purposes." she said. "There's a certain amount of resentment that we now have to maintain what's making our taxes higher."

The Longwood neighbors' plan would permit the Tree Planting Commission to administer the maintenance fund. with direction from Mall butters. Neighbors have also asked that the Commission replace another three beech trees by 1985.
Work on the Mall is expected to begin next spring, once Town Meeting approves the plan.

to_have_and_to_hold.meta_title: 1902: To have and to hold | Longwood Mall
to_have_and_to_hold.meta_description: The 1902 Sears family deed that gave Longwood Mall to the Town of Brookline.
to_have_and_to_hold.title: 1902: To have and to hold
paragraphs: The Sears family “remise, release and forever quitclaim unto the said inhabitants of the Town of Brookline, the following described parcels of land situate in said Brookline…”
The parcels included Longwood Mall, Winthrop Square, Knyvet Square and Mason Square.

paragraphs.html: A habendum clause is a clause in a deed or lease that defines the type of interest and rights to be enjoyed by the grantee or lessee.

In a deed, a habendum clause usually begins with the words "to have and to hold". This phrase is the translation of the Latin habendum et tenendum that historically commenced these clauses in deeds. Technically speaking, the "to have" (Latin: habendum) is separate from the "to hold" (Latin: tenendum), such that the tenendum clause is sometimes considered a separate concept.

paragraphs: Historically, the habendum clause dealt with "the quantity of interest or estate which the grantee was to have in the property granted", while the tenendum clause addressed "the tenure upon or under which it was to be held". Put differently, the habendum deals with the relationship between the possessor and the land—how the land is to be had—while the tenendum deals with the relationship between the possessor and his immediately superior lord—how the land is to be held.
The obsolescence of land tenure, however, renders this distinction mostly historical and academic.

paragraphs.html: The provisions of the habendum clause must agree with those stated in the granting clause. For example, if the grantor conveys a time share interest or an interest less than fee simple absolute, the habendum clause would specify the owner's rights as well as how those rights are limited (a specific time frame or certain prohibited activities, for instance).

paragraphs: Many states, such as Pennsylvania, require a deed to have a habendum clause in order for the deed to be officially recorded and recognized by the Recorder of Deeds.

rose_garden_playground.meta_title: How did the Rose Garden Park become a playground? | Longwood Mall
rose_garden_playground.meta_description: A question about the Sears deed and Winthrop Square led to a history lesson from the Brookline Historical Society.
rose_garden_playground.title: How did the Rose Garden Park become a playground?

paragraphs.html: At the annual Brookline GreenSpace Alliance meeting in May, Ken Liss from the Brookline Historical Society gave a fascinating presentation about the history of playgrounds in Brookline.

paragraphs: I had a question about the Sears deed from 1902, which gave four parcels of land Longwood Mall, Winthrop Square, Knyvet Square and Mason Square to the Town of Brookline.

"This conveyance is made upon the express agreement and stipulations that the parcels of land hereinfore described shall be laid out by the proper authorities of the Town of Brookline s public parks..., and shall never be used for the purpose of a playground, as distinguished from a public park." But Winthrop Square, also know to many of us as the "Rose Garden Park", is now a playground, so I was wondering how that happened, given the terms of the 1902 deed.

Ken didn't know off the top of his head, but I followed up with him the next day and he was able to get to the bottom of the issue. Originally, Winthrop Square was only the southern portion of the park we know today. The ball field to the north of the playground equipment was acquired later in 1909. The playground equipment was added sometime between 1950-1952.

The addition of the playground equipment was possibly a technical violation of the stipulations in the 1902 Sears deed, but that playground has been a valuable part of the community for many years. When my children were younger, we would go to that park quite often. The three distinct sections (a playground, an athletic field, and a Rose Garden) make it a very unique and versatile spot in Brookline.

items.title: June 8 event celebrates Longwood Mall's community and future
items.summary: More than 110 neighbors gathered on June 8 and heard Brookline's Tree Warden report that the Beech Leaf Disease treatments appear to be working.
paragraphs: More than 110 people from across Brookline gathered under the European Beech trees on the evening of June 8, 2026, and heard some very good news. Brookline's Tree Warden and Urban Forestry Manager, Jack Schleifer, explained that the Beech Leaf Disease treatments appear to be working: there is little visible evidence of BLD in Longwood Mall today.

Jack also put the condition of the trees in context. Some of the older beeches are not in perfect health, but that does not necessarily mean BLD is taking hold. Many are very old, and some are dealing with age-related decline or other diseases that have affected beeches for years. The plan is to keep monitoring carefully and to pursue maintenance that may help the more stressed trees.

The event was sponsored by the Brookline GreenSpace Alliance (BGSA) and Friends of Longwood Mall. BGSA president Sean Lynn Jones opened the evening, Rob Schoen of Friends of Longwood Mall spoke about the park's long history, and Ellen Golde, one of the group's founders, shared the story of its origins in the early 1980s and its decades of work to protect the park.
After questions, Jack led a guided tour of the park. The evening ended with cookies, conversation, and Jack planting two tiny Japanese Beech saplings.
Thank you to everyone who came out. The turnout, the questions, and the energy around the park all give real reason to be optimistic about Longwood Mall's future.

items.title: Two new European Beeches planted along Chatham Street
items.summary: Two young Fagus sylvatica trees were planted along Chatham Street in the first week of June as part of Longwood Mall's long-term diversification plan.

paragraphs.html: In the first week of June, two young Fagus sylvatica (European Beeches) were planted along Chatham Street between Hawes Street and Borland Street.

paragraphs: Planting some young European Beech trees is part of the diversification plan for Longwood Mall. Most of the existing European Beeches are already mature, and many are very old. Adding a younger generation now gives the park a better chance of still having large, mature European Beeches in the future.

The broader plan also includes planting other species, so Longwood Mall is not dependent on a single kind of tree. These two new European Beeches help preserve the historic character of the park while the overall tree canopy becomes more age-diverse and species-diverse.

items.title: Beech Leaf Disease (BLD) update
items.summary: A conversation with UMass Amherst Beech Leaf Disease expert Nick Brazee helped clarify treatment options and new planting decisions for Longwood Mall.

paragraphs.html: A recent report by Nick Brazee, a Beech Leaf Disease expert at UMass Amherst, ended with a statement that concerned some of us: "At this time, new plantings of American and European beech are not recommended." Since our plan includes planting some new European Beeches, I spoke with Nick about his report.

paragraphs: Nick generally does not recommend planting new European or American Beech where the trees will not be closely monitored and treated and there are plenty of other options. But he agreed that planting some new European Beeches is reasonable at Longwood Mall, given our treatment plans and the desire to preserve the park's history.

Nick was encouraging about the effectiveness of BLD treatments and supportive of our strategic plan. He has great confidence in the researchers at Bartlett Tree Experts, whom Jack Schleifer has been consulting on the plan.

We will continue the foliar spray treatments this summer, as we have for the last three summers; they seem to have been very effective in controlling BLD. The latest research suggests only two treatments a year are needed (down from three or four), at concentrations as low as 2–4 oz of Broadform per 100 gallons of water.

Research suggests the injectable Arbortect 20-S is the most effective treatment available. We hope to start a trial on some of the healthier trees, though it may not happen until next year. Nick told me early results on the UMass campus show the trees tolerating the injection wounds much better than expected.

Some trees may not look very healthy as they bud this season. That is not necessarily a sign of BLD: many of the trees are very old and also suffer from Beech Bark disease and canker. The tell-tale sign of BLD is banding on the leaves (see photo below). If you see significant banding like this, please let me know and I'll share it with Jack. We also plan root-collar excavations on some trees, and Jack is getting quotes for phosphorus treatments to help the less healthy trees recover.

images.alt: Beech leaf showing banding associated with Beech Leaf Disease

items.title: New tree plantings coming to Longwood Mall
items.summary: Friends of Longwood Mall plan to plant new trees this spring, including Japanese Beech saplings and two young European Beech trees.
paragraphs: We plan to plant new trees in the park this spring. It has been a long time since any new trees have been planted in the park. When new trees have been planted in the past, they were almost exclusively European Beeches, maintaining the monoculture that has existed for many years at Longwood Mall.
Modern arboriculture tells us that monocultures create significant ecological risks, the most critical being their vulnerability to pests and diseases. Our strategic plan is to diversify the park:

items: Plant Japanese Beech saplings. Japanese Beeches are believed to be immune to BLD, but still share some of the same Beech characteristics of the European Beeches. Jack has secured 10 small saplings for Brookline and we plan to plant some of them at Longwood Mall. Because of their small size, we may need to do some fencing around these young trees.

Plant young European Beech trees. Most of the European Beech trees in the park are quite old, some of them more than 150 years old. By planting new European Beeches, we are taking a calculated risk that we can control the progression of BLD and investing now in a new generation of European Beeches for age diversification. Jack has obtained two young European Beeches for spring planting.

Plant non-Beech species. We have identified some species of trees that we think would fit well in the park. Jack is especially interested in planting chestnut trees. There is a disease-resistant cultivar that is not yet available but expected to be soon. We hope to plant some of these in the park next year.

images.alt: Young trees ready for planting at Longwood Mall

items.title: Brookline applies for a Massachusetts biodiversity grant
items.summary: Brookline applied for a Massachusetts Community Biodiversity Grant to support Longwood Mall's long-term tree health and biodiversity plan.

paragraphs.html: Brookline submitted an application in December of 2025 for a $91,000 Massachusetts Community Biodiversity Grant to support Longwood Mall's long-term tree health and biodiversity plan.

paragraphs: The proposal connected Longwood Mall to the state's biodiversity goals in four ways:

items.html: Protect: The project would protect a rare genetic resource in European Beech trees imported from Europe between 1830 and 1850. Charles Sprague Sargent, founder of the Arnold Arboretum, called them "the finest exotic trees which have been planted in greater Boston and probably the finest grove of European Beech in the United States." These trees are threatened by Beech Leaf Disease, which is caused by an invasive nematode and has been devastating beech tree populations across the Northeast.

Restore: Through evidence-based Beech Leaf Disease treatments and targeted arboricultural care, the project would restore tree health by addressing both the disease and the underlying conditions that make trees vulnerable to it. According to the Bartlett report, less than 70% of the trees are currently in good condition and the trend is negative due to the increasing age of the trees. With new plantings, BLD treatments, root-collar excavations, phosphite treatments, and other essential maintenance, we believe the park can be restored to good health for future generations.

Sustain: The project would sustain an ecosystem that has existed for nearly 200 years. The mature beech trees provide important ecosystem services, including carbon sequestration, stormwater management, air quality improvement, urban heat island mitigation, and habitat for native species. Brookline's challenging 2026 budget will put real constraints on the Town's ability to protect the park, so alternative funding sources could help ensure that Longwood Mall is protected during a difficult fiscal period.

Connect: Longwood Mall exemplifies the "Nature in Neighborhoods" theme. It is a publicly accessible green space where Brookline residents, workers from the nearby Longwood Medical Area, and residents of nearby Environmental Justice neighborhoods can experience remarkable nature without leaving the urban core. It connects people to nature in their neighborhood and to the natural and cultural history of Brookline.

paragraphs.html: Unfortunately, Longwood Mall did not receive a Massachusetts Biodiversity Grant. The email Jack received said there were more than 200 applications, so our chances of being selected were a lot lower than we expected when we applied. This press release indicated that 12 projects were funded for a total of $1.1 million dollars.

paragraphs: We will continue to submit grant applications to help fund maintenance and treatment of Longwood Mall.

items.title: Brookline hires Jack Schleifer as Urban Forest Manager
items.summary: Brookline has named Jack Schleifer as its new Urban Forest Manager.

paragraphs.html: From Brookline.News

paragraphs: "Jack Schleifer has been named Brookline’s new Urban Forest Manager, according to a press release from Commissioner Erin Chute of the Department of Public Works. Schleifer will begin the role on July 14.

Schleifer holds a master’s degree from the Yale School of the Environment and has a background in both municipal and environmental nonprofit work. Most recently, he served as Field Operations Manager at the Emerald Necklace Conservancy, where he led an urban forestry program and collaborated with local and state agencies on tree health and maintenance across the Emerald Necklace park system.
In Brookline, Schleifer will focus on stewarding the town’s tree canopy and improving climate resiliency through public engagement and partnerships with the community.
He is filling a role left by Tom Brady, who departed for the city of Watertown in 2023 after more than 20 years on the job in Brookline."

items.title: December 11 community meeting on the future of Longwood Mall
items.summary: Tree Warden Tom Brady introduced Arbortect 20-S, a newly approved injectable treatment, at a December 11 community meeting on the park's future.
paragraphs: At a December 11 community meeting at the Church of Our Saviour, Tree Warden Tom Brady introduced Arbortect 20-S, a newly approved injectable treatment for Beech Leaf Disease, as a promising next step for the trees. Turnout was strong despite 3–4 inches of rain and 50 mph wind gusts. Alexandra Vecchio, Acting Director of Parks and Open Space and Director of Sustainability, also attended.

Tom walked through Brookline's experience with BLD and how he has worked with Bartlett Tree Experts and Dr. Beth Brantley, a leading researcher in BLD treatment, as everyone's understanding of the disease has grown.

Arbortect was approved for use on beech trees only in the last six months. Unlike Broadform, the foliar spray we have been using, it is injected directly into the roots once every 2–3 years. It has been used successfully for many years against Dutch Elm disease and has now been shown to be very effective against BLD. Tom tempered expectations: older trees already stressed by other diseases, such as Beech Bark disease and bleeding canker, may not respond to any BLD treatment.

We also discussed replacing trees that have died or may need to be removed, including planting species other than European Beech given the risk from BLD. Community Preservation Act (CPA) funds may help pay for new plantings.

The evening was bittersweet, as Tom will soon be leaving Brookline, which complicates plans for a long-term strategy for the park. We agreed to continue BLD treatments, including Arbortect for trees that are good candidates, and to meet with the new Tree Warden before deciding on new plantings, hopefully early in 2025. New trees will be a priority, but for a grove around 180 years old, the long-term direction deserves careful, deliberate decisions.
Thank you to Tom Brady and Alexandra Vecchio for attending, and to the Church of Our Saviour for hosting us.

images.alt: Tom Brady speaking at the December 2024 Longwood Mall community meeting

items.title: Tree Warden Tom Brady is leaving Brookline
items.summary: Tom Brady, Brookline's Conservation Administrator, Tree Warden, and Town Arborist, is leaving Brookline after 23 years of service.
paragraphs: Tom Brady, Brookline's Conservation Administrator, Tree Warden, and Town Arborist, is leaving Brookline after 23 years of service. He has taken a new job as the Director of Public Works in Watertown. Tom was named Massachusetts Conservation Administrator of the Year in 2021.

Tom has been an amazing partner with the Friends of Longwood Mall. In recent years, he has been on the front lines of the battle versus Beech Leaf Disease, working with Bartlett Tree Experts to provide critical treatments for the trees. While this is a huge loss for Brookline, we are happy for Tom, as his new position is an exciting new career opportunity and also a significantly easier commute for him. We are very grateful for Tom's service to the Brookline community and wish him all the best!

A search is underway for Tom's replacement. Tom will connect his successor with his contacts at Bartlett. The Friends of Longwood Mall will work with the new Tree Warden to ensure that the preservation of Longwood Mall stays on track during this challenging period.

images.alt: Tom Brady at Longwood Mall

items.title: Community meeting on December 11 about the future of Longwood Mall
items.summary: An in-person community meeting about the future of Longwood Mall was held at 7 p.m. on December 11, 2024, at the Church of Our Saviour.
paragraphs: We will hold an in-person community meeting about the future of Longwood Mall at 7 p.m. on December 11, 2024, in the Lawrence Room of the Church of Our Saviour (25 Monmouth St.), which has generously offered the space.

Tom Brady, Brookline's arborist, conservation administrator, and tree warden, will give a quick update on the health of the park's trees, discuss long-term options, and listen to feedback from the community. One important topic will be diversifying the park by replacing lost trees with species other than European Beech, given its vulnerability to Beech Leaf Disease.

If you missed the July information session, I encourage you to watch the recording first. That session covered what the experts are seeing in the park; this one is for discussing options and hearing from the community.
There will be no Zoom option. If you cannot attend, please reach out to me and I will be happy to recap the meeting and collect your feedback. Hope to see you there!

items.title: First BLD treatment of 2024
items.summary: Bartlett Tree Experts administered Beech Leaf Disease treatments to the trees of Longwood Mall on August 1.
paragraphs: [Update: The town administered 4 BLD treatments between August 1 and September 30.]

On August 1, Bartlett Tree Experts administered Beech Leaf Disease treatments to the trees of Longwood Mall. These were the first treatments given this year, and they were administered under the supervision of Tom Brady from the Parks and Open Space Division of Brookline DPW.

As the experts at the July 15 webinar discussed, the treatments given last year were largely successful at containing the spread and severity of the disease in Longwood Mall. At this point, the goal of the treatments is to control BLD, not to eradicate it.

The treatment given was Broadform, which is the same treatment we administered last year. Broadform is currently the only effective treatment available to us for Beech Leaf Disease. The continued use of Broadform will likely be discussed as we explore long-term strategies for preserving Longwood Mall. Please reach out to me if you have any information or opinions about the use of Broadform in the park.

items.title: Article on Longwood Mall in BGSA's Place magazine
items.summary: The Brookline GreenSpace Alliance asked for an article about Longwood Mall for the 2023 Spring/Summer issue of Place.
paragraphs: The Brookline GreenSpace Alliance (BGSA) asked me to write an article about Longwood Mall for the 2023 Spring/Summer issue of Place, their biannual publication.

paragraphs.html: Preserving Longwood Mall: An Urban Oasis in Brookline

Here long before any of us were born and hopefully remaining long after we are all gone, Longwood Mall stands as one of Brookline's most treasured landmarks. Located less than half a mile from Coolidge Corner, this 2.5-acre linear park serves as an urban oasis that both beautifies the neighborhood and unifies our community.

In the 1840s, David Sears brought European Beech trees (Fagus sylvatica) back from England and planted them on the land that would eventually become Longwood Mall. This picturesque grove is considered by many to be the oldest collection of European Beech trees in North America. In 1902, the family of David Sears generously deeded Longwood Mall and three other parcels of land to Brookline, ensuring their preservation as public parks.

Eighty years later in 1982, Longwood Mall was not in good condition. Cuts to the forestry budget had resulted in the trees being neglected for over two decades, leaving them in desperate need of pruning and cultivation. Led by Ellen Golde, a group of dedicated Brookline citizens raised $20,000 (equivalent to $62,000 in 2023!) to revitalize the trees and establish an annual maintenance program.

This initiative marked the birth of the Friends of Longwood Mall, who later received a Massachusetts Historical Commission Preservation Award in 1984. Since then, Ellen has been working closely with the Brookline Parks Department to ensure that the trees survive and thrive.

Fast forward forty more years, and Longwood Mall is facing a new threat. A new tree disease, Beech Leaf Disease (BLD), has been decimating Beech trees from Ohio to Maine in recent years. Last year, BLD tragically took the life of a historic Beech tree on Freeman St. (by the former St. Aidan's church). Fortunately, none of Longwood Mall's trees have shown symptoms of BLD yet, but community intervention may be the key to preventing an outbreak.

Thankfully, scientists and arborists recently have made significant progress in understanding BLD and have developed a new treatment. Last year, Friends of Longwood Mall raised money from the neighborhood to administer this treatment to the trees. Additionally, we received an $8,500 grant to treat the trees from the Brookline GreenSpace Alliance, as part of the Park Initiative Program. Although it is too early to know how effective the treatments have been, there is reason for optimism.

Unfortunately, the Parks Department did need to remove two of the park's trees in February. These trees were not infected by BLD but were suffering from other maladies and had become a safety hazard for visitors and the other trees. These removals are not done lightly and only done after a thorough assessment by the Tree Warden in consultation with other experts. In the spring, Friends of Longwood Mall will raise money to plant new trees.

It is sad to see the old trees removed and each tree is a living thing that we will strive to protect, but sometimes it can be helpful to take a longer-term perspective. We can think of Longwood Mall as an interconnected whole, where all the trees will eventually die (European Beeches typically live for around 200 years), but new trees will be planted and cared for.
With this approach, we can hope to preserve Longwood Mall indefinitely, so that many future generations of Brookline residents can enjoy the park as we have.

items.title: Two trees removed from Longwood Mall
items.summary: On February 21 and 22, 2023, two of the trees were removed from Longwood Mall.
paragraphs: On February 21 and 22, 2023, two of the trees were removed from the Longwood Mall. Tom Brady, Brookline's Arborist and Tree Warden, had this to say about the removals:

"These removal actions are never undertaken without great thought and consideration. In this case these two trees have been assessed by a total of six certified arborists both from within our department and representatives from three separate tree care firms. All of the arborists were consistent in the recommendation for removal and replacement at this time.

We are grateful for the decades long partnership with the neighborhood in our collective stewardship of the Mall. I would note we have begun the process of securing Beech trees to replace those being removed to ensure the new plantings can be completed this Spring season."
Friends of Longwood Mall will be raising money in the spring to help finance the new plantings. It is sad to see the old trees go, but we will plant new ones and the cycle continues on.

"Nature is a teacher of life, and the cycle of death and rebirth is one of its greatest lessons. It reminds us that change is inevitable and that we must learn to adapt and evolve to survive." - Steve Irwin

items.title: BLD treatment for the trees
items.summary: In the fall of 2022, the trees of Longwood Mall were treated for Beech Leaf Disease and Beech Canker disease.
paragraphs: In fall 2022, the trees of Longwood Mall were treated for Beech Leaf Disease and Beech Canker disease. Treatments were funded through cooperative efforts of the neighborhood and the town. Additionally, the trees were pruned and the entire mall was aerated to help improve access to water and nutrients. Aeration also helps reduce soil compaction, which inhibits the growth of root systems.
Avoiding soil compaction is also why ball playing is not allowed on the mall, in case you were ever wondering.

items.title: Friends of Longwood Mall joins the Brookline GreenSpace Alliance
items.summary: Friends of Longwood Mall formally joined the Brookline GreenSpace Alliance and received a Park Initiative Program Grant.
paragraphs: Friends of Longwood Mall formally joined the Brookline GreenSpace Alliance (BGSA) as a park organization in the summer of 2022. We applied for a Park Initiative Program Grant and were awarded a grant for $8,500 for BLD treatments of the trees on Longwood Mall. These grants are available to Brookline park organizations thanks to funding obtained by our State Representative Tommy Vitolo.
The BGSA does great work to protect and enhance Brookline's green spaces. Please consider joining the organization!

bld.title: Beech Leaf Disease

page_sections.title: About the disease

paragraphs.html: Beech Leaf Disease (BLD) is caused by a microscopic roundworm, the nematode Litylenchus crenatae mccannii, that lives and feeds inside beech leaves. The first sign is dark green banding between the leaf veins, usually on lower branches. Over several years, leaves shrink, curl, and drop early, buds fail, and the canopy thins.

paragraphs: Young trees can die within a few years. Large, mature trees like the beeches of Longwood Mall decline more slowly, which gives time to treat them. The disease affects both the native American beech and the European beech planted here.
BLD was first found in Lake County, Ohio, in 2012 and has spread across the Northeast, reaching Massachusetts in 2020. Birds, insects, and people may all help move the nematodes from tree to tree.
There is no cure, but treatment can hold the disease back. At Longwood Mall, foliar spray treatments every summer since 2022 appear to be keeping it in check.

paragraphs.html: Sources: Wikipedia, US Forest Service, and UMass Amherst.

hero.description: Beech Leaf Disease is the central ecological threat discussed across the recent Longwood Mall updates. This page gathers the essential background, selected treatment notes, and reliable outside resources.

current_note.title: This site's treatment notes currently run through December 2024
current_note.body: The legacy material we transferred includes treatment discussions from fall 2022 through late 2024, including the July 2024 webinar, the August-September 2024 treatment cycle, and the December 2024 community meeting about longer-term options.

summary_cards.title: Cause
summary_cards.text: BLD is associated with a foliar nematode, Litylenchus crenatae mccannii, that feeds within beech leaves and disrupts healthy growth.

summary_cards.title: Symptoms
summary_cards.text: Typical symptoms include dark interveinal striping, thinning canopy, reduced new growth, and broader decline, especially in younger trees.

summary_cards.title: Range
summary_cards.text: First identified in Ohio in 2012, BLD has spread widely across the Northeast, including Massachusetts.

updates.title: Treatments appear to be working
updates.text: At the June 8 community event, Tree Warden Jack Schleifer reported little visible evidence of BLD in the park.

bld.description: What Beech Leaf Disease is, how it affects the trees of Longwood Mall, and what is being done to protect them.

at_a_glance.title: What it is
at_a_glance.text: A disease of beech trees caused by a microscopic nematode that feeds inside the leaves. It was first found in Ohio in 2012 and reached Massachusetts in 2020.

at_a_glance.title: Status at Longwood Mall
at_a_glance.text: As of June 2026, Brookline's Tree Warden reports little visible evidence of the disease in the grove. Some older trees show age-related decline.

at_a_glance.title: What is being done
at_a_glance.text: Foliar spray treatments each summer since 2022, close monitoring, a planned trial of the injectable Arbortect 20-S, and new plantings.

at_a_glance.title: How you can help
at_a_glance.text: Support the treatment and planting fund, and help keep people off trunks and branches, which stresses already-vulnerable trees.

getting_there.title: By public transit
getting_there.text: Longwood Mall is one block from the Hawes Street stop on the MBTA Green Line C branch, about a five-minute walk. From the stop, walk south on Hawes Street to Beech Road.

getting_there.title: By car
getting_there.text: There is no parking lot. Parking is not allowed on Beech Road or Chatham Street on weekdays before 11 a.m. Street parking on the surrounding residential streets is limited and follows posted Brookline rules, including the town's overnight parking ban.

getting_there.title: On foot or by bike
getting_there.text: The park sits in a residential neighborhood near the Longwood Medical Area and Coolidge Corner. Please walk bikes on the lawn.
